title: The Antiderivative and the Constant of Integration
quickIdea: Integration reverses differentiation: every antiderivative of f differs from every other by a constant, and a definite integral cancels that constant away.
remember: F is an antiderivative of f when F'(x) = f(x). The indefinite integral writes the whole family: the integral of f(x) dx is F(x) + C.

The standard forms that GATE actually uses: x^n integrates to x^(n+1)/(n+1) for n not equal to -1; 1/x integrates to ln|x|; e^x to e^x; sin x to -cos x; cos x to sin x; sec^2 x to tan x; 1/(1+x^2) to arctan x; a constant k to kx.
Check an antiderivative by differentiating it - that check is faster than re-deriving and catches every sign error.
In a definite integral the constant cancels: (F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a), so any one antiderivative gives the same number.
x^(-1) is the single power the rule refuses, because n + 1 would be zero; that is why 1/x needs the logarithm.

example.prompt: Find the integral of 3x^2 - 4x + 1 with respect to x, and check it.
example.work: Integrate term by term: 3x^2 gives x^3, -4x gives -2x^2, and 1 gives x. So the family is x^3 - 2x^2 + x + C. Differentiating gives 3x^2 - 4x + 1 back.
example.answer: x^3 - 2x^2 + x + C, and the derivative of that is the original integrand.

gateAngle: GATE never asks for an indefinite integral on its own; it asks for a definite value, so the antiderivative table has to be automatic. Every previous-year question in this topic starts by recognising one of the standard forms - 2015 Set 1 Q.44 recognises the derivative of 1/x inside the integrand, 2014 Set 3 Q.47 recognises that x^2 cos x needs a technique rather than a table entry.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does the indefinite integral of 1/x need the absolute value, ln|x|, while the integral of x^2 does not need one?
variations.answer: Because the antiderivative must work on both sides of zero, where 1/x is defined but x is negative.
variations.why: d/dx ln|x| equals 1/x for every x other than 0: for negative x the chain rule contributes the derivative of |x|, which is -1, and the two minus signs cancel. For x^2 no such domain problem exists, since x^(n+1)/(n+1) is defined wherever x^n is.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: If the integral of f(x) dx is F(x) + C, what is the integral of f(2x) dx?
variations.why: Differentiate F(2x)/2 and the chain rule returns f(2x). The variation tests whether the constant of integration is understood as bookkeeping rather than as part of the answer: the factor 1/2 comes from the inner derivative, not from C.

trap.what: Writing x^n/(n) with n = 0 for the integral of 1/x, or dropping the constant on an indefinite integral.
trap.why: The power rule divides by n + 1, which is zero when n = -1, so that case has no power answer at all; and an indefinite integral is a family, so a single function is only one member of it.
trap.counterexample: Differentiating ln|x| gives 1/x, while differentiating x^0/0 is meaningless. And the two antiderivatives x^2 and x^2 + 7 both differentiate to 2x, so quoting only x^2 for the integral of 2x dx is incomplete.

check.question: Evaluate the definite integral of 1 from 1 to 3, and say which part of the antiderivative you used.
check.explanation: An antiderivative of 1 is x, so the value is 3 - 1 = 2. Geometrically it is a rectangle of width 2 and height 1. The constant never appears: it would have cancelled.
